source_caption:
To fully unleash his unparalleled comedic versatility, Eddie Murphy buried himself under layers of groundbreaking prosthetic makeup to play multiple wildly different characters—most iconically, Randy Watson, the aggressively confident, deeply untalented lead singer of the fictional soul band “Sexual Chocolate.” Collaborating with legendary special effects artist Rick Baker, Murphy completely vanished into the role of the washed-up, Jheri-curled lounge singer. By delivering a hilariously tone-deaf, brutally off-beat rendition of Whitney Houston’s “The Greatest Love of All” and ending with an utterly unearned, dramatic mic drop, Murphy anchored one of the most unforgettable sequences in cinematic comedy. He masterfully proves that true comedic genius isn’t just about the writing; it is about an absolute, fearless, and unflinching commitment to the bit, no matter how absurd.
⠀
Coming to America (1988), directed by John Landis, starring Eddie Murphy, Arsenio Hall, James Earl Jones. An extremely pampered, incredibly wealthy African prince rejects an arranged marriage and secretly travels to the gritty borough of Queens, New York, going undercover as a humble fast-food worker in a desperate, hilarious quest to find a woman who will genuinely love him for his character rather than his immense royal fortune.

source_details.synopsis: Coming to America is a 1988 American romantic comedy film directed by John Landis, based on a story originally created by Eddie Murphy, written by David Sheffield and Barry W. Blaustein, and starring Murphy (in various roles), Arsenio Hall (also in various roles), James Earl Jones, John Amos, Madge Sinclair and Shari Headley. It tells the story of Akeem Joffer, the crown prince of the fictional African nation of Zamunda who travels to the United States in the hopes of finding a woman he can marry and will love him for who he is, not for his status or for having been trained to please him.
